Consider the following statements about Wildlife Protection Act, 1972:
1. Schedule-I covers endangered species that need rigorous protection. The species are granted protection from poaching, killing, trading etc.
2. Species that are not endangered are included under Schedule-II.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.questionText: Consider the following statements about Wildlife Protection Act, 1972: 1. Schedule-I covers endangered species that need rigorous protection. The species are granted protection from poaching, killing, trading etc. 2. Species that are not endangered are included under Schedule-II. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanationHtml:
(a)
• Animals under Schedule II are also accorded high protection with the prohibition on their trade. They cannot be hunted except under threat to human life or if they are suffering from a disease/ disorder that goes beyond recovery.
• Species that are not endangered are included under Schedule III and Schedule IV.

questions.subject: Civil Engineering
questions.questionMarkup:
Statement (I): Fuel cells work like batteries, but they do not run down or need recharging.
Statement (II): Fuel cells produce electricity and heat as long as fuel is supplied.
questions.questionText: Statement (I): Fuel cells work like batteries, but they do not run down or need recharging. Statement (II): Fuel cells produce electricity and heat as long as fuel is supplied.
questions.explanationHtml:
(a)
• Fuel cells work like batteries, but they do not run down or need recharging. They produce electricity and heat as long as fuel is supplied.
• (a)fuel cell consists of two electrodes—a negative electrode (or anode) and a positive electrode (or cathode)—sandwiched around an electrolyte.
• (a)fuel, such as hydrogen, is fed to the anode, and air is fed to the cathode. In a hydrogen fuel cell, a catalyst at the anode separates hydrogen molecules into protons and electrons, which take different paths to the cathode.
• The electrons go through an external circuit, creating a flow of electricity. The protons migrate through the electrolyte to the cathode, where they unite with oxygen and the electrons to produce water and heat.
